1-1.text: Part one. How light travels. ... A light source gives out its own light. The Sun, a lamp and a candle are all light sources.

1-2.text: The Moon is not a light source. It looks bright because it reflects light from the Sun.

1-3.text: Light travels in straight lines. We draw it as a ray: a straight line with an arrow on it.

1-4.text: Light is very fast: it travels about three hundred thousand kilometres every second. Light from the Sun reaches the Earth in about 8 minutes.

1-5.text: We see things when light from a source bounces off them and goes into our eyes. Nothing comes out of our eyes.

2-1.text: Part two. Materials and shadows. ... Transparent materials, like clear glass, let almost all light through. You can see clearly through them.

2-2.text: Translucent materials, like tracing paper, let some light through but scatter it. Things look blurry through them.

2-3.text: Opaque materials, like wood, metal and card, let no light through at all.

2-4.text: An opaque ball blocks the light. Light travels in straight lines and can't bend round it, so a dark shadow forms behind it.

2-5.text: Move the ball closer to the lamp and it blocks more of the light, so the shadow gets bigger.

3-1.text: Part three. Reflection. ... When light hits a mirror, it bounces off. This is called reflection.

3-2.text: Where the ray hits the mirror, we draw a dashed line at right angles to the mirror. This line is called the normal.

3-3.text: The angle between the ray going in and the normal is the angle of incidence. Here it is 40 degrees.

3-4.text: The law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. So the angle of reflection is 40 degrees too.

3-5.text: A smooth, shiny surface reflects light neatly, so you can see an image in it. A rough surface, like paper, scatters light in all directions.

4-1.text: Part four. Refraction. ... Light slows down when it goes from air into glass or water.

4-2.text: If light hits the glass at an angle, it changes direction. This bending of light is called refraction.

4-3.text: Going into the glass, the ray bends towards the normal. Coming out into the air, it bends away from the normal.

4-4.text: Refraction makes a straw in water look bent. Light from the straw bends as it leaves the water, so the straw looks as if it is in a different place.

5-1.text: Part five. Colour. ... White light is really a mix of colours. A prism splits it into a spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

5-2.text: This is called dispersion. Each colour refracts by a different amount: violet bends the most and red bends the least.

5-3.text: A red apple reflects red light into our eyes. It absorbs all the other colours.

5-4.text: White things reflect all the colours. Black things absorb all the colours.

5-5.text: A coloured filter only lets its own colour through. A red filter absorbs every other colour, so only red light comes out.

5-6.text: Shine pure blue light on a red apple and it looks black. It absorbs the blue light, and there is no red light for it to reflect.
